a: The Great Wall of China has a long and complex history spanning over 2,000 years. The first major walls were built during the Qin Dynasty (221-206 BCE) under Emperor Qin Shi Huang, who connected and expanded existing fortifications built by earlier Warring States to protect against nomadic invasions from the north. However, most of the surviving wall we see today was built during the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644 CE), when the wall was extensively rebuilt, reinforced, and extended using brick and stone masonry rather than the earlier rammed earth construction. The Ming Wall stretches approximately 8,850 kilometers (5,500 miles) from Shanhaiguan on the Bohai Sea in the east to Jiayuguan in the Gobi Desert in the west. Contrary to popular belief, the wall was not continuously manned but consisted of strategic watchtowers, garrison stations, and beacon towers that could signal troops using smoke and fire. The wall served multiple purposes: defense against raids, border control, regulation of trade along the Silk Road, and as a psychological barrier. After the Ming Dynasty fell to the Manchu Qing Dynasty in 1644, the wall lost its military significance since the Qing expanded beyond it, and it gradually fell into disrepair. Today, it is a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the most iconic structures in the world.
